title: Security review - pen test results & patching cadence - Crestline Bank
next_steps: Liam to send consolidated pen-test report and remediation plan
Marisol to provide patch impact notes and rollback guidance
Schedule follow-up review week of 2026-03-16 to validate remediation and retest
action_items: Liam Chen - send consolidated pen-test report + remediation plan - due 2026-03-06
Marisol Vega - produce patch impact/compatibility notes for our runtime and share mitigation scripts - due 2026-03-09
Rajesh Kumar - confirm maintenance window constraints and preferred patch cadence - due 2026-03-05
Emily Dawson - share compliance checklist and SOC2 evidence requirements - due 2026-03-10
summary: Review of external pen test findings and discussion of vulnerability management, secure SDLC and patch cadence. Customer concern around patch/testing timelines, data residency and audit evidence. Agreed follow-ups: share full pen test PDF, remediation plan, patch impact notes and schedule retest.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we got the team from Redwood here, I'm Liam Chen, AE. We'll run through the pen test findings and next steps. Marisol will walk the technical items.
[00:00:15] Nina Patel: Thanks Liam, appreciate you fitting us in. We got the external pen test back last week and a few red flags around exposed admin endpoints and a couple of high-risk vulns we want to understand impact for, especially for our private deployment.
[00:00:30] Marisol Vega: Hi Nina, thanks, we read the report this morning. First call out, a couple of the items labeled high are related to default config endpoints that are only present in older agent versions we shipped last year - we patched them server-side for hosted but for Dedicated/Private customers the remediation is a config patch.
[00:00:48] Rajesh Kumar: Quick clar - when you say "patched server-side for hosted" does that mean our private deployment won't get the fix unless we take action? Our compliance team requires a documented patch cadence.
[00:01:02] Marisol Vega: Correct, for private you control the upgrade. We can provide a hotfix and a patch script; we also have recommended Kubernetes manifests for zero-downtime. We'll share a step-by-step and a preflight checklist.
[00:01:18] Marcus Li: What's the expected downtime for the hotfix? Our SLAs for certain endpoints don't allow more than 5 minutes of interruption.
[00:01:29] Owen Park: For the specific config endpoint fix it's usually a rolling restart of pods, typically 90-120s per pod; with a 3-node pool you can do a rolling upgrade with virtually no outage if you have proper readiness/liveness probes. We'll include specific commands.
[00:01:50] Emily Dawson: The pen test flagged an auth bypass scenario (they referenced CVE-ish id like CX-2025-113 but the naming was inconsistent). Can you map that to your CVE references or internal tracker?
[00:02:05] Marisol Vega: We believe that's the token validation edge case we patched in v2.3.7; internal tracker ref INF-2025-87. We'll include mapping to CVE entries if applicable; sometimes pen testers use their own shorthand.
[00:02:20] Sarah Brooks: From legal/compliance: we need to know whether audit logs for admin actions are immutable and exportable for our SOC2 evidence.
[00:02:32] Liam Chen: Good question - audit logs are shipped to the customer's configured destination. For private deployments you can connect to your existing SIEM - we support syslog/CloudWatch/Splunk. Logs are append-only on our side and we support signed export bundles for attestation. We'll include the evidence pack instructions.
[00:02:52] Nina Patel: Data residency is also a blocker. Some findings reference data left in tmp storage during uploads - can you confirm encrypted at rest and whether ephemeral temp files are wiped?
[00:03:06] Marisol Vega: All data volumes support AES-256 at rest via customer-provided KMS or Redwood-managed KMS. For private, you can plug in your KMS (we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM integrations). Temp files are written to transient ephemeral volumes and we run a secure wipe on pod termination; the specific issue looked like it was a misconfigured retention policy in their test harness.
[00:03:29] Rajesh Kumar: On KMS, do you support key rotation automation? Our policy is 90-day rotation and we need automated rotation without rebuild.
[00:03:40] Marisol Vega: Yes, we support key aliasing; you can rotate keys in your KMS and we honor the alias. For deeper automation we can provide a rotation lambda example and docs.
[00:03:52] Nina Patel: Walk us through vulnerability management - how do you triage severity, and what's your SLA for critical fixes?
[00:04:03] Marisol Vega: We categorize criticals as CVSS 9-10 and anything with active exploit evidence. For hosted customers we backport fixes and push within 72 hours for criticals; for private/dedicated we publish an advisory and provide a hotfix with recommended remediations. We also provide mitigation suggestions if customers can't patch immediately.
[00:04:23] Marcus Li: What's your testing/QA for patches? We can't accept something that breaks our workloads.
[00:04:30] Owen Park: Patches go through our CI/CD pipeline with unit and integration tests, then canary rollout in our staging fleet and performance regression checks. For private distributions we provide a build artifact and a reproducible test harness so you can run preflight tests.
[00:04:48] Emily Dawson: Do you have a secure SDLC? We need evidence of SAST/DAST and supply chain scanning for dependencies.
[00:04:58] Marisol Vega: Yes, we run SAST on PRs (we use a mix of static tools and in-house rules), dependency scanning against OSS manifests, and container image signing. We can share a summary of our SDLC controls and the tooling list for your auditor.
[00:05:13] Nina Patel: The pen test also called out a medium severity path traversal vector on an older file upload handler. Is that covered by the uploader rewrite you mentioned?
[00:05:24] Marisol Vega: It is - we rewrote the handler in v2.3.0 and deployed to hosted; for private we will include the backport. It's low effort to patch, but we'll supply a test case and CVE mapping.
[00:05:37] [00:10:00] Liam Chen: quick pause, we've been talking specifics - want to confirm priorities from your side: regulatory evidence (SOC2), patch cadence/SLA, and minimal downtime during remediation. Correct?
[00:10:12] Nina Patel: Yes, also we need to know what constitutes a verified remediation - will a vendor patch + internal verification be enough, or do we require a retest by the same third-party?
[00:10:24] Sarah Brooks: Legal leans toward a third-party retest for high/critical items if they're in-scope for our regulator.
[00:10:33] Marisol Vega: We can support both: provide remediation artifacts and test cases for your internal retest, and if required we will coordinate with the pen test firm for a retest window. We also offer a Redwood-led verification package for an additional fee.
[00:10:49] Rajesh Kumar: Patch cadence - we run heavy traffic on weekdays. What maintenance windows do you recommend and can you do staggered rollouts?
[00:11:01] Owen Park: We recommend off-peak weekends or 1-4am local time in your region. Our orchestration supports phased rollouts by namespace/node pool so you can limit blast radius. We'll provide sample k8s manifests for canary percentages.
[00:11:17] Marcus Li: If we need to delay patching, what mitigations can we apply?
[00:11:22] Marisol Vega: We recommend layer 7 WAF rules and feature flags to disable vulnerable endpoints. For the specific auth token bug there's a configuration toggle that forces stricter validation we can enable immediately while you schedule the full patch.
[00:11:36] Nina Patel: On audit trail immutability - you mentioned signed bundles. How are they generated and are they acceptable evidence for SOC2 auditors?
[00:11:48] Liam Chen: Signed bundles are SHA-256 signed with our service key and can include log immutability metadata. Many customers have used these bundles as part of SOC2 evidence; we'll attach sample bundles and an auditor-facing note.
[00:12:02] [00:20:00] Emily Dawson: A question about RBAC/SSO - can admins be scoped to only specific models or routes? We need least privilege across teams.
[00:12:12] Marisol Vega: Yes, our RBAC supports granular roles: model-level, route-level, and environment-level permissions. We integrate with SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. We'll send a role matrix and sample policies.
[00:12:28] Rajesh Kumar: Does SCIM handle group sync? We need automatic deprovision when folks leave.
[00:12:34] Marisol Vega: Yes, group and user sync. We support attribute mapping and deprovision events.
[00:12:40] Nina Patel: For encrypted transport and in-flight keys, do you support client-side encryption for sensitive prompts?
[00:12:48] Liam Chen: We don't do full client-side encryption for model inputs today because inference requires plaintext input on the host; however, we do support envelope encryption - you can encrypt certain payloads and manage keys on your side, we can work through a proxy pattern if you require it. For strict regulatory workloads we recommend a private deployment inside your VPC with HSM-backed KMS.
[00:13:11] Marcus Li: Regarding vulnerability triage: will Redwood share CVSS and suggested mitigations in the advisory?
[00:13:17] Marisol Vega: Yes, the advisory will include CVSS score, exploitability notes, recommended config changes, patch steps, and a smoke test.
[00:13:27] Nina Patel: Can you commit to a timeline for the high findings - we need to present to the board next week.
[00:13:35] Liam Chen: We'll commit to sending the consolidated report by 2026-03-06 with proposed remediations and estimated RTF (remediation timeframes). For private customers, remediation ETA depends on your maintenance window but we'll provide a recommended schedule.
[00:13:48] Sarah Brooks: If we accept a maintenance window that causes a service slowdown, do you offer credits?
[00:13:55] Liam Chen: Credits are part of the Dedicated contract negotiations; for Private it's governed by the support addendum. We can note possible credit policy for your legal to review.
[00:14:08] [00:30:00] Marisol Vega: A few technical clarifications from the pen test: 1) The "exposed admin" finding was due to an unauthenticated endpoint only reachable if the operator flag was enabled in older builds. 2) The TLS config issue flagged weak ciphers on the test harness; our default ciphers have been updated across the fleet. 3) The file upload issue is remediated in the new uploader. We'll annotate each finding in the PDF with the patch version and mitigations.
[00:14:34] Rajesh Kumar: Who will own verification once you push the hotfix?
[00:14:38] Marisol Vega: We can do a joint verification session. Our standard is vendor provides fix + reproducible test case, customer runs internal verification, then optional third-party retest. We'll schedule the joint verification during your maintenance window.
[00:14:52] Emily Dawson: We need a clear story for auditors on patch timelines and evidence. What artifacts do you provide?
[00:14:59] Liam Chen: Artifacts: advisory PDF with CVSS mapping, PR/commit links, build artifact checksums, signed log bundle, test cases, and a remediation confirmation email thread. We'll also provide a one-page runbook for auditors.
[00:15:15] Nina Patel: For vulnerability management, do you maintain a public advisories page or private feed?
[00:15:21] Owen Park: We maintain a private vendor advisory feed per customer and public advisories for non-sensitive items. We'll grant Crestline access to the private feed for the duration of remediation.
[00:15:33] Marcus Li: Are there any expected breaking changes for model compatibility when applying the patch?
[00:15:38] Marisol Vega: No breaking model changes; most fixes are runtime/config and shouldn't affect model outputs. We'll provide compatibility matrix and regression test results.
[00:15:49] [00:40:00] Liam Chen: Ok onto next steps real quick - agree we'll: 1) Share consolidated pen-test PDF with our annotations, 2) provide remediation plan and hotfix artifacts, 3) schedule a joint verification + retest window, 4) share SOC2 evidence pack and RBAC policy matrix.
[00:16:05] Nina Patel: That sounds good. Also please include a recommended cadence for security patching we can present to the board.
[00:16:12] Marisol Vega: Typical options: immediate for critical (within 72 hours), weekly security patch batch, monthly maintenance for non-urgent items. You can pick the cadence that fits your change control. We'll include pros/cons.
[00:16:26] Sarah Brooks: We'll need contractual language around time-to-patch for critical vulnerabilities if this moves forward.
[00:16:33] Liam Chen: Understood - we'll draft suggested SLA language for inclusion in the engagement.
[00:16:40] Nina Patel: One more question - do you keep historical audit logs beyond 90 days? Our policy requires 12 months for certain events.
[00:16:49] Owen Park: We have long-term log retention available as an add-on; logs can be exported to your archive and stored for 12+ months. We'll document retention options and costs.
[00:17:02] [00:50:00] Marisol Vega: I'll summarize the technical artifacts we'll send: annotated pen test PDF, hotfix tarball + k8s manifests, smoke tests, rollback steps, SAST/DAST summary, and RBAC role matrix.
[00:17:15] Emily Dawson: Please include a timeline example for a 3-node rollout so we can model the board slide.
[00:17:21] Marisol Vega: Will do.
[00:17:24] Liam Chen: Let's capture action items and owners - we'll send the follow-up email within 24 hours including the next meeting invite.
[00:17:31] Nina Patel: Thanks all, appreciate the clarity. We'll review the materials and aim to align on the maintenance window by 2026-03-05.
[00:17:39] Liam Chen: Great. Thanks everyone.
[00:17:45] [End of transcript]
